Second, we conducted an independent repeat of the GPT-5-mini experiments that used a different prompt with anti-gaming and anti-PyTorch-only instructions (as discussed in Section 6.3). Figure 13 summarizes the observed spread across configurations spanning two model tiers and two agent variants. Each dot is the geomean speedup of one configuration. Boxes show the interquartile range with whiskers extending to min/max. Vertical dashed lines mark the MI baselines.

(1) Performance gains persist despite run-to-run variation. Every GPT-5-mini configuration with μ\muCUTLASS—including the lowest ablation variant (MNTIS at 1.20×1.20\times) and the independent repeat run (1.22×1.22\times)—exceeds the GPT-5 MI baseline of 0.86×0.86\times by at least 40%40\%. The cross-run gap for μ\muCUTLASS + SOL-guided (1.56×→1.22×1.56\times\to 1.22\times, a 0.34×0.34\times shift) falls within the ablation envelope (1.201.20–1.74×1.74\times, a 0.55×0.55\times spread), indicating that the repeat run lies within the observed spread across nearby configurations. Relative variant rankings are preserved across both the repeat run and the ablations: μ\muCUTLASS + SOL-guided remains the strongest, and μ\muCUTLASS consistently provides a large improvement over the corresponding non-DSL variant. The main conclusions from the primary results therefore remain unchanged.

(2) Variation decreases with model capability. GPT-5.2 variants cluster tightly: 5%5\% CV with μ\muCUTLASS and 7%7\% without, across four and five configurations respectively. The corresponding Fast-pp curves in Figure 6(a) are nearly indistinguishable. GPT-5-mini shows wider variation (1313–15%15\% CV), consistent with weaker models exhibiting more sensitivity to agent/prompt configuration and generation randomness.

6.5 Comparison to Prior Work

Figure 14 compares μ\muCUTLASS + SOL-guided across three model tiers against the Sakana AI CUDA Engineer Lange et al. (2025), using the integrity-filtered kernels provided on huggingface as described in Section 5.9. Because the software stack and runtime measurement methodology differ between the two evaluations, we compare against Sakana AI’s reported speedups directly.

Of the 59 evaluation problems, 2 have no correct kernel in the Sakana archive. Of the remaining 57, our LLM-based review accepts 52 kernels (28 No Issue, 24 Minor Issue) and rejects 5 (3 PyTorch-only, 2 Gaming), after evaluating 450 candidate kernels across the fallback review process. The accepted Sakana kernels achieve a geomean speedup of 1.13×1.13\times over their own PyTorch baseline. The 7 problems with no accepted kernel (2 missing, 5 rejected) are assigned speedup zero, counting against Sakana in the Fast-pp comparison.

The Fast-pp curves show a clear separation. All three μ\muCUTLASS + SOL-guided results provide higher speedups compared to the Sakana baseline. Even GPT-5-mini with μ\muCUTLASS + SOL-guided (1.56×1.56\times geomean) substantially outperforms Sakana (1.13×1.13\times), with a higher fraction of problems reaching ≥2×\geq 2\times speedup. GPT-5 (2.07×2.07\times) and GPT-5.2 (2.79×2.79\times) widen the gap further. The comparison highlights that the SOL-guided steering and μ\muCUTLASS DSL provide large gains beyond what a different frontier model alone achieves with an evolutionary search strategy.

If we select the fastest integrity-filtered kernel found for each problem across all our variants and runs, the resulting geomean speedup is 3.91×3.91\times (4.53×4.53\times median), with all 59 problems solved. Figure 14 also includes the FP16 SOL curve (dashed purple), which reaches a 7.46×7.46\times geomean speedup. Closing this gap through adaptive variant selection, multi-variant ensembles, SOL-informed generation, or improved search strategies could yield substantial gains while keeping generation efficient.

7 Conclusion

We evaluated two methods to improve the efficiency of LLM-driven GPU kernel optimization across three model tiers (GPT-5-mini, GPT-5, GPT-5.2). The first is raising the level of abstraction using a domain-specific language, μ\muCUTLASS, that lets the model reason in an optimization space offering high-impact levers while hiding low-level implementation complexity. The grammar is compact enough to be learned entirely in context. The DSL alone turns GPT-5-mini’s flat baseline from a 0.40×0.40\times regression to a 1.27×1.27\times geomean speedup, and benefits all three model tiers, with the largest gains on the weakest model.

The second is Speed-of-Light (SOL) guided optimization steering, which uses first-principles performance bounds to structure the agent’s search. Combined with μ\muCUTLASS, SOL-guided steering reaches 1.56×1.56\times, 2.07×2.07\times, and 2.79×2.79\times geomean speedup on GPT-5-mini, GPT-5, and GPT-5.2, respectively, enabling each model to match or exceed the next tier’s raw-code baseline at lower inference cost. We further employ SOL guidance to improve efficiency by allocating budget to problems that have higher optimization headroom. SOL-guided scheduling saves 19 to 43% of tokens while retaining ≥95%\geq 95\% of geomean speedup, with the best configuration achieving a 1.68×1.68\times efficiency gain.

We found that game detection is crucial for LLM-based code optimization, as LLMs often find loopholes in specifications and produce kernels that appear fast without performing the intended computation. SOL guidance helps here as well, first as a static runtime ceiling to flag physically implausible results, and then to augment the specification for an LLM-based game detector. Without such detection, our results show that reported speedups can be inflated by up to 1.9×1.9\times.

Future work includes automatically discovering compact DSL abstractions for new optimization domains, using per-problem characteristics to choose the most effective agent strategy and budget allocation, integrating integrity feedback into the optimization loop so that agents can correct gaming behavior during search, and applying first-principles performance bounds to steer LLM-based optimization in domains beyond GPU kernels.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Full EBNF Grammar for μ\muCUTLASS

We include the full EBNF grammar used as the reference specification here.

A.2 Example SOL Report

We include a sample SOL report for KernelBench Problem 001 (4096×\times4096 FP32 GEMM) here. The main body uses FP32/TF32 assumptions matching the problem’s declared precision. The FP16 augmentation at the end shows how the bounds tighten when reduced-precision Tensor Cores are assumed, and is used for scheduling and integrity checking.
